analysis.one_liner: Bans forced arbitration of workplace disputes and restores workers' right to join class actions.
analysis.headline: Introduced in June 2024 with 11 Democratic sponsors, the bill was referred to two committees, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for employers to require workers to sign away their right to go to court before a dispute even exists. It also bans forced waivers of the right to join a class or collective lawsuit, and lets workers agree to arbitrate only after a dispute arises, voluntarily, with at least a 45-day waiting period, plain-language notice of their rights, and written consent. It prohibits firing or punishing workers who refuse to arbitrate, and adds these protections to the National Labor Relations Act so workers can file federal charges. The rules cover independent contractors, not just employees.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at companies that use mandatory arbitration agreements — which cover a large share of nonunion private-sector workers — including employees and independent contractors. Anyone with a claim for unpaid wages, discrimination, harassment, or retaliation gets the choice of court instead of a private arbitration process chosen by the employer, and workers hurt by wage violations can pool their claims in class or collective actions again.

how_it_helps.text: Predispute arbitration agreements covering work disputes become unenforceable, so workers cannot be required to arbitrate as a condition of getting or keeping a job.
Predispute waivers of class, collective, or joint claims become unenforceable, restoring workers' ability to band together in Rule 23 class actions and Fair Labor Standards Act collective actions.

Postdispute arbitration is allowed only if it is truly voluntary: not coerced, not a condition of employment, explained in plain language, signed only after at least a 45-day waiting period with affirmative written consent, and the statute of limitations is paused during that wait.
Employers are barred from retaliating against workers who refuse to arbitrate, and workers can sue over such retaliation with attorney's fees and the remedies available under civil rights laws.

The National Labor Relations Act is amended so employers also violate federal labor law by interfering with workers' right to pursue joint or collective claims, and the rules extend to independent contractors regardless of how the employer labels them.

analysis.who_pays: Covered entities — employers of all sizes, plus individuals and firms that engage contractors — lose mandatory arbitration and class-action waivers for workplace disputes, and would face more lawsuits in court, including wage-and-hour class and collective actions. Arbitration providers would lose the steady stream of workplace disputes that mandatory agreements route to them.

drawbacks.text: Employers would lose the private arbitration process that is often faster and cheaper than court, and small businesses especially would face higher litigation costs and exposure to wage-and-hour class actions they can currently block in advance.

More cases moving to court could slow down resolution of individual disputes; the bill preserves arbitration only as a voluntary post-dispute choice with a required 45-day waiting period before consent.
Arbitration provisions in union collective bargaining agreements remain valid, so unionized workers would keep a different system than nonunion workers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and large for workers: mandatory arbitration and class-action waivers currently decide most workplace claims in a private forum the employer selects, with no appeal and no class mechanism, so restoring court access and class rights changes who can actually enforce wage and anti-discrimination laws. The cost falls on employers, who lose a cheaper, private dispute channel and face more litigation — a genuine objection for small businesses — but the bill is drafted carefully, with carve-outs for union contracts and strict safeguards to keep any post-dispute arbitration voluntary.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on June 11, 2024 and sent to the House Judiciary Committee and the House Education and Workforce Committee, but neither committee held a hearing or reported it out, and the full House never voted before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerrold Nadler of New York introduced the Restoring Justice for Workers Act on June 11, 2024, together with Rep. Bobby Scott of Virginia.
The Speaker referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary and, additionally, to the Committee on Education and the Workforce for the parts within each committee's jurisdiction.
Ten House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsors are listed.
The action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote — before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that rely on mandatory arbitration agreements and class-action waivers keep the existing system, since no rule changed. Arbitration providers keep the workplace-dispute business those agreements generate.

for.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it.

for.name: Rep. Robert Scott
for.role: Original co-lead, House Education and Workforce Committee

against.name: Rep. Jim Jordan
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, which sat with the committee from referral until the Congress ended.

against.name: Rep. Virginia Foxx
against.role: Chair, House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred to her committee.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 10 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsors appear on the bill, and Republican committee chairs took no action on it.

industries.note: These employers currently require most of their workforce to arbitrate workplace disputes privately and sign away class-action rights, which cuts off court access for workers with wage, discrimination, and harassment claims. The bill makes those agreements unenforceable and exposes employers to more court litigation, including class actions.
Mandatory pre-dispute agreements route a large volume of workplace disputes to private arbitrators. The bill allows arbitration only as a voluntary post-dispute choice, shrinking that business.
